I'm 66 this year, and these bones aren't what they used to be. My family has about 5 mu of flat land here in Quzhou that we've worked for generations. I only went to primary school, but I know this soil better than any book. Every year I grow winter wheat and summer maize — that's what this land was made for, and I don't have the strength or the cash to gamble on something new.

My wheat went into the ground last October, same improved variety that Old Wang from the next courtyard has been using. Now it's spring, so first thing I'll do is top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up. I use about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu total for the wheat, plus some compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium. Last year Li tried cutting his nitrogen to save money and his wheat turned yellow and thin — I'm not taking that chance. I'd rather spend a bit more than lose the crop. I'll irrigate three times: at green-up, at jointing, and at heading. The water bill hurts, but dry wheat is worthless wheat. I'll spray once for aphids around May if they show up, which they usually do. If the weather holds like it did two years ago, I should get about 450 kg per mu.

Come early June, I'll harvest the wheat and immediately turn around and plant hybrid maize. There's barely a week between crops, so I'll run the rotary tiller quick and get the seed in the ground before the soil dries out. The maize needs about 16 kg nitrogen per mu — I put compound fertilizer down at planting and top-dress with urea at the big trumpet stage. Two irrigations for the corn, and two pesticide sprays: one for weeds right after planting, and one for stem borers later. I expect around 500 kg per mu.

I thought about putting half a mu into garlic like Zhang did — he made good money one year. But at my age, bending down to dig garlic kills my back for a week, and the price jumps around too much. My grandson is in middle school and costs money. Grain prices are steady, and buyers always come to the village. I'll stick to what I know.
